newsitem.title: UK: S&P affirms South Africa's long-term debt ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms South Africa's long-term debt ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it affirmed the Republic of South Africa's BB plus long-term foreign currency rating, which will be assigned to its debut Yankee issue.
S&P also said it affirmed South Africa's BBB plus long-term rating on rand-denominated debt and said the outlook on both ratings remained positive.
S&P said the ratings were supported by expected continuation of South Africa's:
-- Commitment to fiscal and monetary discipline and market-based structural reforms, which was reaffirmed in the government's June 1996 medium-term economic plan;
-- Manageable external debt burden. Net external debt and debt service relative to exports were comparable to the median of sovereigns in the BB foreign currency rating category;
-- Stable and comparatively low rates of inflation; and
-- Strengthening political stability, underpinned by popular political leadership and social resilience.
S&P said creditworthiness remained constrained by:
-- High fiscal deficits and public debt burdens, which limit policy flexibility and constrain economic growth by depressing domestic savings and investment;
-- Weak external liquidity in the context of South Africa's increasing reliance on confidence-sensitive portfolio investment and failure to attract significant foreign direct investment; and
-- Major economic and social distortions fostered under the previous political regime, evidenced by high unemployment and wages and a low- skilled work force.
The government's new medium-term economic program should strengthen South Africa's prospects for faster economic growth if fully implemented.

Firm fiscal and monetary policies, trade reform, gradual reduction of exchange controls, and public sector reform will be continued, but with accelerated reductions in fiscal deficits (from a budgeted 5.1 percent of GDP in 1996-1997 to 4 percent in 1997-1998 and three percent in 1999-2000) and tariffs.

S&P said the post-1993 recovery should continue, though slow down, this and next year, with GDP growth stabilising at somewhat over three percent in 1996 before registering perhaps 2.5 percent in 1997.

Average inflation should continue its post-1991 decline this year, falling to about 8 percent from 8.6 percent last year, but will rise in 1997 to probably under 11 percent, in part because of devaluation-driven wage and price pressures.
The current account deficit is expected to decline to about 2 percent of GDP this year and less next year, limiting the increase in net external debt relative to exports to around 80 percent.

S&P said a ratings upgrade would probably hinge on the extent to which key policies were implemented -- led by sustainable fiscal consolidation, further exchange control liberalisation and asset restructuring -- and accompanied by improved prospects for faster economic and employment growth and stronger external liquidity.
